summary: This informational note describes issues raised by the deployment of Internationalized Domain Names, both at registration time and in use within the DNS. It recommends that the IETF update the IDN-related RFCs, proposes a framework for doing so, and suggests investigating changes to IDNA and its tables.

eli5.summary: Domain names can now use letters from many languages, but that has caused some surprises. This note lists the problems and says the rules should be fixed.

questions: what are confusable characters in domain names
subtitle: The IAB takes stock of problems with internationalized domain names and proposes how the IETF and ICANN should respond.

tldr.problem: After the first years of Internationalized Domain Names (IDNs), problems appeared: look-alike characters, language-dependent matching, and IDNA being tied to Unicode 3.2.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB reviews the issues, then recommends that the IETF update the IDN RFCs with a smaller, inclusion-based character list, plan for newer Unicode versions, and that registries adopt inclusion-based policies and dispute processes.
tldr.outcome: It is Informational advice to the IETF and ICANN. Its recommendations are topics to investigate, not protocol changes.

today: RFC 4690 is an Informational IAB document, and the metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It records the IAB's view as of September 2006 and its recommendations were advice to the IETF and ICANN.

sections.title: IDNs Are Just DNS Names
sections.content:
The IAB writes from the view that IDNs are no more and no less than DNS names, with the same requirements for use, stability and accuracy as traditional hostnames, but a much larger set of permitted characters. They address only a small part of making the Internet equally accessible from all languages.

The DNS itself sets limits that no IDN design can change. There is one and only one owner of each domain name, a positive answer reflects only an exact match (no near matches or searches), and every server must use the same matching criteria because any server might cache responses. The RFC says the goal of stable, predictable and secure references has proven very difficult to satisfy fully, so engineering compromises are needed.
sections.eli5: A web address is like a street address: it has to match exactly, and only one house owns it. Using more alphabets does not change that rule.

sections.title: The IDNA Family of Standards
sections.content:
During 2002 the IETF completed the RFCs that together define IDNs. RFC 3454 defines Stringprep, a generic way to turn a Unicode string into a canonical form. RFC 3490 defines IDNA, the base specification. RFC 3491 defines Nameprep, the Stringprep profile for domain names, which normalizes and case-folds. RFC 3492 defines Punycode, which encodes Unicode as the letter, digit and hyphen (LDH) characters allowed in hostnames.

Unicode is the base character set, and the RFCs explicitly depend on Unicode Version 3.2. At the time of this document there was no established mechanism to move the IDNA RFCs to newer Unicode versions.
sections.eli5: There are four rule books that work together: one cleans up text, one says how to use it in domain names, one makes letters comparable, and one turns fancy letters into plain ones computers can store.

sections.title: Problems with Matching, Scripts and Look-Alikes
sections.content:
The RFC walks through examples. Language-specific matching: U+00F8 and U+00F6 are not equivalent in Unicode, yet many Swedish, Danish and Norwegian speakers treat them as the same, and making them equivalent globally would confuse German users. Multiple scripts: some languages can be written in more than one script, so the same word can take different forms. Normalization: Unicode normalization handles simple character equivalences only, not language-dependent ones, and odd combining sequences give attackers room to spoof if implementations differ.

Other issues are the 'side-of-the-bus problem' (reading a URL from a printed or fleeting display), bidirectional text (IDNA allows European digits in a right-to-left label but prohibits most other mixes), and confusable characters. Look-alike characters can send people to the wrong host, and the RFC notes this has been exploited by attacks such as phishing. It recommends the term 'confusable' rather than 'homograph'. These difficulties cannot be fully removed by algorithms; protocol tuning, registry action and careful user interfaces all help, but some responsibility rests with the user.
sections.eli5: Some letters in different alphabets look the same, like twins. Someone sneaky can use the look-alike to trick you into visiting the wrong place.

sections.title: Moving to New Versions of Unicode
sections.content:
IDNA is far more sensitive to subtle Unicode changes than typical applications. A change that is not strictly additive can be extremely disruptive if a DNS label was defined under the earlier form. The RFC cites a 2004 correction to the normalization definition: some deployed implementations adopted it and others did not, leading to subtle incompatibilities.

This creates a dilemma. Freezing IDNA at a Unicode version that excludes newer scripts is unacceptable, but so is a migration that could invalidate or make ambiguous an existing registered name. Because IDNA normalizes at registration time and compares strings normalized at different times, the RFC says it may even be impossible to guarantee that a source string always normalizes to the same result. If decisions are made quickly, a one-time upgrade to Unicode 4.1 or 5 may be possible; beyond that, upgrades could be painful, possibly needing changed strings in the DNS or a new Punycode prefix.
sections.eli5: The alphabet book keeps getting new pages. If a new edition changes how an old word is spelled, names people already own could stop working, so changes must be made very carefully.

sections.title: Framework and Recommendations
sections.content:
For the IETF, the RFC suggests reviewing RFCs 3454, 3490, 3491 and 3492 and updating, replacing or supplementing them, adapting to the current Unicode version and specifying a path for later ones. It reports a consensus that code points should be listed by inclusion (naming what is permitted) rather than excluding a few, and proposes a design team with IETF, DNS and Unicode Consortium expertise. Section 5 recommends permitting as few characters as possible, dropping non-language characters such as box-drawing, and questioning whether the hyphen should be generalized to other scripts.

For ICANN and registries, the IAB recommends an inclusion-based model for registration characters, developed alongside dispute resolution, and extending such policies to zone administrators at all levels. It also reminds readers that the DNS cannot do near-matching or searching, that IDNs do not remove the ASCII structure of URIs, and that the whois protocol has no standard way to handle non-ASCII text.
sections.eli5: The advice is: allow only the letters we really need, write down who is allowed to register what, and have a plan for settling arguments.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says it is a discussion of IDNs and IDNA issues and raises no new security concerns. It adds that if its recommendations to reduce IDNA complexity, shrink the set of available characters and constrain confusable characters are followed and prove successful, the risks of name spoofing and other problems may be reduced.
sections.eli5: This note does not add new dangers. If its advice is followed, tricking people with look-alike names should get harder.
